# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hide

When choosing where to hide, pick a cell that balances two things: it should not be predictable based on my previous positions, and it should not match the cell I just fired at (since Foxtrot might be tempted to fire back at my last known shooting position). Vary between edge cells and central cells across rounds. Do not stay in the same cell twice in a row.

## Note

Keep notes brief and uninformative. "Steady on station" works. Do not signal your strategy or intentions in notes—they are public and will be used against you. Do not claim cooperation or openness; this is a competitive game and such claims waste your credibility. Save your limited reputation capital for critical moments only.

## Fire

Always fire at your standing order target. Do not deviate unless you have explicit tactical reasoning. When firing, do not fire at the cell you hid in—this makes it too easy for your target to predict your next location if they were paying attention.

## Claim

When the office tells you the true result, claim it truthfully. Always. You have no choice but to match the private result anyway, so there is no advantage to considering dishonesty. Truthful claims preserve your credibility if anything hinges on it later.

## Escort

Do not claim an escort unless you have specific reason to believe it will be reciprocated. Do not claim an escort with a boat that is clearly losing or under threat—it signals an alliance they may resent. Claiming "none" is safe and avoids wasting your nomination on a worthless mutual gain. Only claim an escort when mutual recognition is likely or when you actively want to signal temporary cooperation.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

**Hiding Strategy**
When choosing where to hide, start in central positions (4-6) to balance risk and maintain flexibility. After the first round, track which positions have been fired at and shift away from patterns—if you've hidden in the same cell twice, move to a different zone in round three. Avoid the edges (1, 9) unless you have strong evidence the opponent is searching center.

**Firing Strategy**
Always follow the standing order unless you have concrete tactical reason not to. The standing order exists for coordination; deviating from it without cause creates chaos and wastes ammunition. Fire at your designated target with medium-risk positions (mid-range cells 4-6 initially, then adjust based on hits and misses). Do not fire on Harbor—the payoff penalty is too severe and the threat is credible.

**Claim Discipline**
Always claim the result truthfully as the office tells it to you. You must claim hit when you hit and miss when you miss. This is enforced, not optional, and lying creates disqualification risk. Your score depends on accumulating points fairly, not on deception.

**Escort Claims**
This is where I failed repeatedly: I claimed "none" when I should have been tracking mutual escort opportunities. Watch for patterns in other boats' notes and positioning. If another boat appears to be shadowing you or signaling coordination, name them as your escort to try to secure 5 points each round. Never claim an escort you cannot justify or reciprocate. Do not default to "none"—actively seek one mutual escort pairing per round with the boat most likely to name you back.

**Notes**
Post steady, consistent notes to build trust and predictability in your own positioning. Notes are not strategy—they are signals of stability. Keep them simple: "steady on station" or similar. Do not use notes to deceive.

**Scoring Priority**
You ended at +7 after one hit (4 points) plus some escort points. The escort points came from somewhere but you did not track them. Next time: count your points carefully each round and reverse-engineer which escorts were reciprocated. Prioritize consistency in escort pairing over chasing new alliances. A reliable mutual escort every other round beats random claims.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**Hiding:**
When choosing where to hide, don't just pick the middle. Vary your position unpredictably across rounds. Track which cells opponents have fired at you in recently and avoid those. If an opponent just missed, they're likely to try an adjacent cell or shift their strategy—anticipate this and move further away. Avoid repeating the same hiding location across rounds, as opponents will learn your patterns.

**Targeting:**
Follow the standing order to fire at the designated next boat. Don't deviate from this without a strong tactical reason. When you fire, choose a cell that reflects where you think your target will hide based on their recent history and behavior patterns, not just your own hiding spot.

**Claiming:**
Always file your true result claim. Lying about your shots undermines the game's information structure and doesn't give you any advantage you can act on later. The office knows the truth anyway, and maintaining honesty keeps your signals credible if you ever need to influence other players' perceptions.

**Escort claims:**
Track which boats have consistently cooperated or acted in mutual interest. Establish mutual escort partnerships with specific boats and maintain them across rounds to generate steady 5-point gains for both of you. Don't claim escort with random boats—pick one and stay consistent unless they stop reciprocating.

**Strategic priorities:**
Your lead is fragile. Don't assume your current score insulates you. Harbor is a constant threat with the payroll jettison penalty—never fire on Harbor. Focus fire pressure on whoever is most threatening (highest score or most accurate shots against you). Watch for boats forming escort partnerships and consider whether joining them would serve you better than competing.

**Final round:**
In round 6, you gain nothing from deception or changed behavior. Play it straight. Your decisions at that point don't compound—there's no future round to prepare for.
